newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST - Primary dealers see no Fed move until 97.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Primary dealers see no Fed move until 97.

text.p: In a stunning change in sentiment, economists are in unanimous agreement that the Federal Reserve will keep short-term interest rates steady through year-end, with a chance rates will be unchanged for many months to come.
In a Reuters survey, economists at all 37 primary dealerships said the Fed will keep rates unchanged at both the November 13 and the December 20 Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meetings.
"Five-and-a-quarter percent federal funds here we come on Super Bowl Sunday" January 26, said William Sullivan, director of money markets research at Dean Witter Reynolds Inc.

The results contrast to a similar poll taken just prior to the September 24 FOMC meeting, when 17 dealers forecast a quarter-point rate hike at that meeting. Another 17 predicted steady policy, and three said it was a toss-up.

Seven weeks later, many economists said it is possible the Fed may not have to raise rates at all. A wave of economic data the past couple of weeks showed an economy moving along at a solid pace, with no imminent signs of overheating.

Third quarter Gross Domestic Product (GDP) grew at a 2.2 percent rate, with final sales rising just 0.3. Also, a 0.6 percent rise in the third-quarter Employment Cost Index (ECI) suggests wages are not rising as rapidly as many thought.
"The ECI last last week showed no compelling reason to tighten," said Joseph Liro, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy Securities Corp.

"Third quarter GDP was benign enough and there's a sluggish start to fourth quarter retail sales that unless we get a distinct pickup in terms of fourth quarter demand, and until we see more pressing evidence of wage pressures turning into consumer inflation, they'll (the Fed) stay on the sidelines and wait until that evidence materializes," he said.
But despite the current tame inflation/moderate growth scenario, most economists still expect the economy to improve enough to force the Fed to raise rates sometime next year.

Of the 37 dealers, 24 said the next Fed move will be a tightening, with 20 of those estimating a tightening will occur as early as the first quarter of 1997. However, some aren't too confident with their forecasts.

"We're out of the woods for the moment, becasuse this is a situation where the economy at the moment is running at about the speed limit. So the next move you don't know," said John Williams, chief global economist at Bankers Trust Co.
"At the moment, there's no reason for the Fed to move in either direction unless the economy starts moving significantly above 2.0 percent or significantly below 2.0 percent," he added.

Meanwhile, eight economists predicted the next Fed move as an ease, with the other four forecasting the Fed on hold for a while. In September, 32 dealers anticipated a rate hike, and three a rate decrease as the Fed's next eventual move.

"The consumer is going to come back so we're going to seriously talk about a tightening after Christmas," said William Dudley, chief economist at Goldman, Sachs & Co Inc. He noted that consumer balance sheets are in the "best shape in years," with household' assets up $4.0 trillion, much higher than the $600 billion rise in debt the past six quarters.

Given the economic uncertainty, 27 primary dealer economists expect the Fed to leave the asymmetric bias toward tightening in place next week. "The unemployment rate (at 5.2 percent) is below the natural rate, so they can't take it off," said Marc Wanshel, economist at J.P. Morgan & Co Inc.

Months ago, it had seemed the economy was growing fast enough that wage pressures would bring on consumer price inflation to warrant a Fed move. As late as September, 20 dealers still predicted a 5.75 percent fed funds rate by year end.
"When they didn't go in September, the Fed showed greater tolerance for risk on inflation than we thought they had," said James Glassman, senior economist at Chase Securities Inc.

As such, some economists don't expect the Fed to move at all in the near future, which would challenge the longest period without a Fed move in recent years. The Fed has been on hold now for nine months since it eased rates in early February. The longest stretch recently was 16 months from the Fed's ease in September 1992 to the tightening in February 1994.
Most, though, aren't thinking about an ease.

"There's no smoking gun, so there's no strong incentive to do it (tighten) now," said Mitchell Held, chief economist at Smith Barney Inc. "But non-union wages and non-sales wages continue to accelerate. They lose nothing by sitting now, but at some point the Fed may have to take a step."
